Abstract
Dysarthria, a speech disorder commonly associated with neurological conditions, poses 
challenges in early detection and accurate diagnosis. This study addresses these challenges 
by implementing preprocessing steps, such as noise reduction and normalization, to en­
hance the quality of raw speech signals and extract relevant features. Scalogram images 
generated through wavelet transform effectively capture the time-frequency characteristics 
of the speech signal, offering a visual representation of the spectral content over time and 
providing valuable insights into speech abnormalities related to dysarthria. Fine-tuned 
deep learning models, including pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) archi­
tectures like VGG19, DenseNet-121, Xception, and a modified InceptionV3, were opti­
mized with specific hyperparameters using training and validation sets. Transfer learning 
enables these models to adapt features from general image classification tasks to classify 
dysarthric speech signals better. The study evaluates the models using two public datas­
ets TORGO and UA-Speech and a third dataset collected by the authors and verified by 
medical practitioners. The results reveal that the CNN models achieve an accuracy (acc) 
range of 90% to 99%, an F1-score range of 0.95 to 0.99, and a recall range of 0.96 to 
0.99, outperforming traditional methods in dysarthria detection. These findings highlight 
the effectiveness of the proposed approach, leveraging deep learning and scalogram im­
ages to advance early diagnosis and healthcare outcomes for individuals with dysarthria.

1  Introduction
Speech is a complex motor activity that involves the coordination of various muscles in the 
vocal tract to produce sounds. These muscles include the muscles of the larynx, tongue, lips, 
and velum. The combined movement of these organs creates disturbances in the air within 
the respiratory passages, generating the sources needed for speech production. Speech pro­
duction relies on the intricate coordination of multiple muscles in the vocal tract, including 
those in the larynx, tongue, lips, and velum. Each of these muscles plays a specific role in 
shaping and regulating airflow to create the diverse range of sounds that form human speech 
(Dos et al. 2020).
Dysarthria is a speech impairment that arises from muscle weakness. This weakness is 
typically the result of injury to the neurological system, which is responsible for certain 
muscles. When the complex network of muscles responsible for articulating speech is com­
promised, it affects the muscles used for speech, making it difficult for individuals to control 
and coordinate the movements needed for clear and intelligible speech. This can result in 
slurred or delayed speech, trouble with articulation, and changes in voice quality. Dysarthria 
is classified into numerous forms, each of which is connected with a different neurological 
problem. Peripheral dysarthria specifically refers to issues affecting the tongue, larynx, and 
adjacent muscles as a result of harm to the speech-related organs.The degree of the speech 
impairment is correlated with the amount of stress that is exerted on the muscles that are 
linked with speaking (Calvo et al. 2021).
Dysarthria is a common speech disorder that affects the production of speech due to 
muscle weakness or paralysis. It can result in slurred speech, difficulty pronouncing words, 
and a decreased ability to control pitch, volume, and rhythm of speech. Early recognition 
and appropriate intervention for dysarthria are crucial in order to improve communication 
abilities in individuals with this disorder. By assessing and categorizing dysarthria, speech 
and language treatment can be tailored to address the specific impairments present in each 
individual (Yorkston and Beukelman 2013).
Machine learning models using speech impairment datasets have shown promise in early 
Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) detection. Sustained vowel phonation, promising 
results with jitter and shimmer feature extraction, has been effective in classifying ALS and 
healthy controls. A support vector machine classifier achieved 98.5% accuracy in classify­
ing ALS/HC (Shabber et al. 2023b).
In a review paper (Shabber et al. 2023a) authors explored the potential of machine 
learning for diagnosing speech disorders, specifically focusing on dysarthria, a common 
symptom in conditions like ALS, Cerebral Palsy (CP), and Parkinson’s Disease (PD). Early 
diagnosis of ALS is especially critical because it affects not only speech production but also 
breathing and swallowing. The paper highlights a promising technique called "sustained 
vowel phonation" for differentiating between these disorders and healthy speech. It delves 
into various machine-learning approaches that have been used to analyze speech patterns to 
diagnose ALS, PD, and CP.
Scalograms offer a powerful tool to visualize how speech signals change in frequency 
over time. They are especially useful for understanding how different aspects of speech, 
like phonemes and prosody, affect frequency. Techniques like Short-time Fourier transform 
(STFT) and continuous wavelet transform (CWT) allow us to see these changes and high­

This study investigates the efficacy of scalograms images for classifying dysarthric 
speech disorders. Pre-trained CNNs, traditionally employed for image recognition, offer 
potential for improved speech signal processing in dysarthria detection. This research 
explores the application of transfer learning to utilize these pre-trained models for the 
specific task of dysarthria classification. To ensure the generalizability of the findings, the 
proposed approach will be evaluated across a variety of data using three distinct speech 
datasets.
In contrast to existing research that primarily focuses on comparative analyses of estab­
lished models on a single dataset, this study incorporates three diverse datasets: two publicly 
available collections and one hospital-derived dataset collected specifically for this research. 
This comprehensive approach facilitates a robust assessment of model performance across a 
broader range of data distributions.
Furthermore, in this work a modification to the CNN architecture is specifically designed 
for dysarthric speech detection, aiming to enhance both accuracy and robustness is pro­
posed. Through the combination of multiple Datasets and the introduction of innovative 
model designs, strengthens the bridge between theoretical research and practical applica­
tions, ultimately aiming to advance assistive technologies for speech impairments.
This study aims to address this gap by conducting a detailed analysis of the effectiveness 
of pre-trained CNNs in this specific domain.

This study proposes a deep-learning approach for dysarthric speech classification. The 
approach utilizes a comprehensive data strategy, utilizing 2 public datasets with 1 hospital-
collected dataset to capture a broader range of speech patterns. Scalograms are employed to 
extract informative features, aiding in the identification of speech variations associated with 
dysarthria. Pre-trained Convolutional Neural Networks are employed to exploit their image 
recognition capabilities through transfer learning. A novel CNN modification specifically 
designed for dysarthric speech classification is proposed. This modification aims to further 
enhance the model’s ability to accurately and robustly identify dysarthric speech patterns.

3.1  Dataset 1 (TORGO)
The TORGO dataset (Rudzicz et al. 2012), known for its diverse collection of speech 
recordings from individuals with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and cerebral palsy, provides 
a foundational resource with a range of speech characteristics. This dataset includes both 
dysarthric and healthy individuals, with specific emphasis on elements relevant to dysarthria 
detection, such as digits, international radio alphabet words, high-frequency corpus words, 
words from dysarthria assessment tools, and phonetically contrasting pairs. Recordings 
were conducted at a sampling rate of 16 kHz using a head-mounted microphone, preserving 
speech clarity. In terms of demographic distribution, the dysarthric group includes 3 females 
and 5 males, while the healthy group consists of 3 females and 4 males. This dataset thus 
offers valuable diversity but lacks detailed information on age, disease duration, or medica­
tion use.
3.2  Dataset 2 (UA-Speech)
The Universal Access Dysarthric Speech (UA-Speech) database (Hasegawa-Johnson et al. 
2011) focuses on individuals with cerebral palsy, providing a different perspective on dys­
arthric speech. This dataset comprises 13 healthy and 15 dysarthric (ranging from 18 to 68 
years) speakers with usable data it offers significant insights into speech affected by cerebral 
palsy. Each speaker repeated commonly used words (e.g., digits and computer commands) 
three times, resulting in a total of 465 utterances per speaker. Recordings were also made at 
16 kHz using microphones optimized for signal-to-noise ratio. The demographic distribu­
tion includes 4 females and 9 males in the dysarthric group and 4 females and 11 males in 
the healthy group. Similar to TORGO, the UA-Speech dataset lacks precise data on partici­
pants’ age range, disease duration, and treatment status, which limits control over potential 
confounding factors in speech characteristics.

3.3  Dataset 3 (custom hospital-collected dataset)
To analyze speech impairments in Parkinson’s disease (PD), a custom dataset was developed 
through collaboration with two hospitals, under the supervision of a neurologist. Ethical 
guidelines were strictly adhered to during data collection. The dataset includes recordings 
from 84 participants, balanced across 42 healthy individuals and 42 individuals diagnosed

For healthy individuals, the group comprises 13 females and 29 males, while the dysar­

was categorized into mild, moderate, and severe levels. This categorization was determined 
by the neurologist based on clinical evaluations, which considered motor symptoms, speech 
impairments, and their impact on daily functioning. Disease duration was also recorded 
as an additional measure to complement the assessment. Severity levels were distributed 
across various age ranges, ensuring representation of early, mid, and advanced stages of 
Parkinson’s disease progression.

4.1  Wavelet-based conversion of dysarthric speech to images
Dysarthric speech, characterized by speech abnormalities such as stuttering, irregular pauses, 
and inaccurate articulation, requires detailed analysis in the frequency domain to understand 
its spectral characteristics. Wavelet transformation is a useful tool for analyzing data that 
has features at different scales. Unlike other techniques that might focus only on high or low 
frequencies, wavelets can capture both. Imagine you’re examining a photograph. Wavelets 
can provide a detailed breakdown of the background colors (low-frequency) while also 
allowing you to zoom in and see the sharp edges and textures (high-frequency) with good 
clarity. This makes wavelets valuable for studying signals that change over time or images 
with intricate details (Mallat 2009). This multi-resolution view enables a comprehensive 
examination of the signal’s spectral features, which is crucial for effective analysis and 
processing.
Compared to conventional methods like STFT and Single Frequency Filtered Fourier 
Transform (SFF-FT), wavelet transformation is particularly advantageous for localizing 
transient features in non-stationary signals like dysarthric speech (Vainio and Rajala 2013). 
Its ability to capture both time and frequency information simultaneously makes it a suitable 
choice for analyzing speech signals with varying characteristics. The CWT (Bassam and 
Al-Amri 2022) is essential in this context because it assesses how closely a signal matches 
an analysis function, usually a wavelet, at various scales and positions. This allows for the 
identification of important features in the signal across different frequency bands, providing 
valuable insights into the underlying speech abnormalities.
Scalograms were selected as the primary time-frequency representation due to their sig­
nificant advantages over traditional methods like spectrograms and MFCCs, especially for

This approach capitalizes on the ability of wavelets to decompose speech signals into 
time-frequency representations, unveiling the unique spectral characteristics of dysarthric 
speech. The analysis involves segmenting the speech signal and applying the Continu­
ous Wavelet Transform (CWT) to each segment. Scalograms are then generated using the 
absolute values of the CWT coefficients, effectively capturing the time-varying spectral 
characteristics of the speech (Mallat 2009). These scalogram images can be subsequently 
utilized as input for pre-trained Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) (Shanmugapriya 
and Mohan 2023). This wavelet-CNN framework offers a robust and informative analysis 
method for dysarthric speech, enabling researchers to delve deeper into the characteristics 
of the disorder and develop more effective detection and classification algorithms.
The speech waveform is represented as a series of scalograms, generated based on the 
waveform’s length and the degree of overlap. Selecting an appropriate wavelet function 
is crucial for effective speech analysis (Rioul and Vetterli 2019). While wavelets like the 
Mexican hat are commonly used in image analysis, they are less suitable for speech signals 
due to poor formant resolution. For this reason, wavelet functions such as Daubechies, Mor­
let, and Morse are considered more appropriate for speech signal processing. This research 
employs the Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) with the Morse wavelet function for 
dysarthric speech analysis (Tan 1996; Olhede and Walden 2002).
The Morse wavelet was chosen for its unique ability to provide balanced time-frequency 
localization, making it highly effective for analyzing the non-stationary nature of dysar­
thric speech. Dysarthric speech exhibits rapid fluctuations, irregular patterns, and frequency 
shifts that require a wavelet capable of capturing fine temporal and spectral details. Com­
pared to Daubechies wavelets, which offer strong time localization but limited frequency 
resolution, and Morlet wavelets, which lack adaptability for complex speech signals, the 
Morse wavelet provides superior flexibility in addressing these challenges (Shanmugapriya 
and Mohan 2023). Its adaptability facilitates detailed analysis across multiple scales, captur­
ing high-frequency components and low-frequency variations essential for identifying vocal 
abnormalities.
Preliminary tests demonstrated that the Morse wavelet achieved higher classification 
accuracy when applied to scalogram representations of dysarthric speech, further validat­
ing its suitability for this study. This combination of adaptability, resolution, and empirical 
effectiveness makes the Morse wavelet an optimal choice for this analysis.

Careful selection of parameters enables the Morse wavelet function to effectively analyze 
the time-frequency characteristics of speech signals, especially in studying dysarthria. The 
scalogram, calculated from the magnitude or power of wavelet coefficients, provides a two-
dimensional visual representation of the signal’s time-frequency distribution, with time on 
one axis and frequency on the other. Brighter regions in the scalogram highlight higher 
energy in specific frequency components over time. For instance, a high-pitched piano note

frequency and harmonics, with intensity reflecting the note’s strength at that time.

In this paper, scalograms serve as the fundamental input for the dysarthria speech classifica­

a range of CNN-based architectures. Pre-trained CNNs are adapted for dysarthria speech 
classification using transfer learning. This adaptation facilitates the extraction of intricate 
scalogram features essential for achieving accurate classification. The choice of pre-trained 
CNNs includes VGG19, DenseNet, Xception, and a modified version of Inception v3. These 
architectures have demonstrated remarkable success in various natural image classification

datasets such as ImageNet, which has resulted in their ability to extract highly informative 
and discriminative features from images which aligns intending to achieve high accuracy in 
classifying dysarthric speech signals based on scalogram representations.
The process of retraining these selected pre-trained networks and performing inference 
in this study involves three key steps, each critical to the overall success of the classification 
task. These steps include: Preprocessing, Pretraining and Evaluation.
4.2.1  Speech preprocessing for CNN input
Preprocessing is essential in preparing speech signals for effective scalogram generation 
and accurate classification. In this study, preprocessing ensures that the signal retains criti­
cal information while minimizing noise-induced distortions. To remove background noise 
without compromising the integrity of speech features, spectral subtraction was applied, a 
technique that estimates stationary noise and subtracts it from the speech signal’s spectrum. 
By preserving essential speech frequencies, spectral subtraction aids in maintaining the 
quality of phonetic details crucial for dysarthria classification. Min-max normalization was 
applied to scale signal amplitudes, reducing the impact of recording variations and ensuring 
amplitude consistency across samples. This step enhances model robustness and minimizes 
biases from amplitude variations.
The next step involves converting the speech signal into a format suitable for input into 
CNN models. This involves converting the raw speech signal data into images, such as 
scalograms, which represent the characteristics of dysarthric speech signals. This step facili­
tates the generation of scalograms, which are visual representations of the signal’s time-fre­
quency content. These scalograms, essentially images illustrating frequency changes over 
time, often have standardized sizes like 227 × 227 pixels.

DenseNet (Tareq and Ahmed 2022) is known for its dense connectivity pattern. Unlike 
typical neural networks where information travels in a single direction through each layer, 
DenseNet allows every layer to directly communicate with all the others. This creates a web 
of connections that ensures information flows freely throughout the entire network. This 
study employed a DenseNet-121 variant, typically used for image classification tasks, to 
process the scalogram representation (a 2D image) of the speech signal. Figure 4 represents

Xception, proposed by François Chollet (Chollet 2017), introduces a novel approach to 
convolutional layers known as depthwise separable convolutions. This approach decouples 
the spatial and channel-wise convolutions, leading to more efficient learning and reduced 
computational complexity. Xception has demonstrated state-of-the-art performance on vari­
ous computer vision tasks. Figure 5 represents the xception architecture that was utilized 
for this work.
VGG-19 (Kim and Loizou 2022), an extension of the VGG-16 architecture, is known 
for its simplicity and uniformity. It uses 3 × 3 convolutional filters throughout the network, 
along with 2x2 max-pooling layers with stride 2. While effective for image classification

5  Results and discussion
In this study, speech signals from three distinct datasets were processed to generate scalo­
gram images, which were subsequently classified using a DenseNet, Xception, VGG-19, 
and modified Inception-v3 deep learning model. The workflow involved noise-reduced, 
normalized speech signals transformed into scalogram representations using Morse wave­
let transformations. These scalograms effectively captured the time-frequency features 
essential for differentiating dysarthric and healthy speech patterns. Performance metrics, 
including accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score, were calculated based on a 5-fold cross-
validation setup to assess model robustness across the datasets.
The research investigates the impact of utilizing scalogram representations of speech 
signals on the classification efficacy of various pre-trained neural networks. This analy­
sis is conducted utilizing the Adam optimization algorithm to fine-tune the networks for 
optimal performance in speech classification tasks. Different batch sizes and various num­
bers of epochs are also considered in the analysis. Adam is found to perform better than 
other learning algorithms, such as Stochastic Gradient Descent Method (SGDM) and RMS 
Prop, as it combines their advantages. The evaluation of different optimization algorithms 
revealed that Adam consistently achieved better performance across all three datasets for 
dysarthric speech classification. Compared to Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), Adam 
yielded accuracy improvements ranging from 3.00% to 13.25%. Similarly, Adam outper­
formed RMSprop by a margin of 1.90% to 5.26% in terms of accuracy. These findings sug­
gest that Adam’s efficacy stems from its capability to adaptively adjust learning rates during 
the training process. This characteristic allows Adam to potentially navigate challenging 
optimization landscapes encountered in dysarthric speech classification tasks, ultimately 
leading to high performance.
The dataset was divided into 80% for training and 20% for testing to evaluate the mod­

robustness. In this approach, the training data was split into five equal subsets, where, in 
each iteration, four subsets were used for training, and the remaining subset was used for 
validation. This process was repeated across all folds, with results averaged to ensure a reli­

6  Conclusion
In conclusion, this study investigated the effectiveness of pre-trained convolutional neural 
networks for categorizing dysarthric speech disorders using scalogram images extracted 
from speech signals. In this investigation of deep learning for dysarthria identification, 
the proposed modified InceptionV3 architecture achieved impressive results. Preprocess­
ing steps enhanced speech signals for feature extraction, and transfer learning from pre-
trained CNNs (VGG19, DenseNet-121, Xception) empowered the models. The proposed 
model consistently surpassed established models on unseen testing data across all datasets. 
On established datasets (TORGO, UA-Speech), it achieved performance with a smaller 
gap between training and testing accuracy compared to established CNNs (e.g., 92.56% 
accuracy on TORGO). It also exhibited a good balance between precision (identifying true 
dysarthria cases) and recall (minimizing false negatives) on the TORGO dataset (precision: 
0.8043, recall: 0.9539). The UA-speech dataset results showcased exceptional performance 
with the highest accuracy (96.78%), precision (0.9681), and F1-score (0.9678). Notably, 
the custom dataset (Dataset-3), potentially capturing disease-specific speech features, led 
to improved performance across all models. The proposed model continued its dominance, 
achieving the highest accuracy (99.07%), precision (0.9902), and F1-score (0.9906) on the 
Dataset-3. These quantitative results highlight the promise of deep learning, particularly the 
proposed modified InceptionV3 architecture, for accurate dysarthria identification, espe­
cially when analyzing custom datasets designed for specific applications. This suggests that 
the proposed method has the potential to be an effective tool for categorizing dysarthric 
speech disorders using scalogram features. Overall, the findings of this study highlight the 
potential of pre-trained CNNs for improving speech signal processing in the context of 
dysarthric speech disorders.
Future research could aim to refine the proposed method further, enhancing its perfor­
mance and exploring its potential for broader speech-related applications. This includes 
expanding the model for multi-class classification to distinguish between ALS, PD, and CP, 
thus broadening its relevance across various neurological disorders.

Abstract: Dysarthria, a speech disorder commonly associated with neurological conditions, poses challenges in early detection and accurate diagnosis. This study addresses these challenges by implementing preprocessing steps, such as noise reduction and normalization, to en­ hance the quality of raw speech signals and extract relevant features. Scalogram images generated through wavelet transform effectively capture the time-frequency characteristics of the speech signal, offering a visual representation of the spectral content over time and providing valuable insights into speech abnormalities related to dysarthria. Fine-tuned deep learning models, including pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) archi­ tectures like VGG19, DenseNet-121, Xception, and a modified InceptionV3, were opti­ mized with specific hyperparameters using training and validation sets. Transfer learning enables these models to adapt features from general image classification tasks to classify dysarthric speech signals better. The study evaluates the models using two public datas­ ets TORGO and UA-Speech and a third dataset collected by the authors and verified by medical practitioners. The results reveal that the CNN models achieve an accuracy (acc) range of 90% to 99%, an F1-score range of 0.95 to 0.99, and a recall range of 0.96 to 0.99, outperforming traditional methods in dysarthria detection. These findings highlight the effectiveness of the proposed approach, leveraging deep learning and scalogram im­ ages to advance early diagnosis and healthcare outcomes for individuals with dysarthria.
